archetype.name: Cup Contender (shot-share juggernaut)
archetype.definition: A team that controls the puck and the chances more completely than anyone in the league, and turns that control into a margin wide enough to carry it through the cold stretches every team hits.

report.headline: Same Carolina shot machine, now with the bounces going its way too
report.take:
Carolina is doing what Carolina always does, only more of it. The Hurricanes lead the league in 5-on-5 expected-goal share (59.8%) and shot-attempt share (59%). They also lead in shots on goal per game (33.3) and rank second in fewest allowed (22.4). That is a team keeping the puck in the other end for most of every night. The 14-3-2 record and the No. 1 spot on the site follow from that, not from good fortune.

The record is built on margin. Carolina's Goal Diff / GP of 1.74 is the best in the league, the season differential sits at +33, and Pts vs Goal Diff is actually slightly negative (-0.6). If anything the standings have under-credited the goal differential, despite an overtime loss in Edmonton and one-goal wins over Boston and Columbus. Scoring has climbed since October: 5.5 goals a game in November, and 25 goals in the last five, including a 9-2 over Chicago and a 7-0 over Winnipeg. That has pushed the offense to second in the league while the defense stays fourth.

The numbers hide one change. This club has spent recent seasons dominating play and getting little reward at the finishing end: PDO of 99.1, 98.3 and 98.4 the last three years. This year it is 102, and the all-situations version is 102.2, sixth in the league. The process is the familiar one; last year's expected-goal share was 56.3%, and this year's is higher still. What is new is pucks going in, including depth finishing like Mark Jankowski's 8 goals on 28 shots. Some of that will cool. Because the shot share underneath is the real thing, a cooling means a very good team rather than a historic one.

The other question is in goal. Pyotr Kochetkov has been elite (.920, +8.7 GSAx, third on the goalie tab). Brandon Bussi has started seven games at .869 and -4.2 GSAx. The team-level B+ grade blends the two. How the starts get split from here matters more than any regression in shooting luck. The 129-point pace will not hold, but a top seed and a deep spring run are well within reach.

strengths.title: League-best control of play
strengths.body: Carolina owns the best 5-on-5 expected-goal and shot-attempt shares in the league. It pairs the most shots on goal per game with the second-fewest allowed. That comes from the system and from depth: nearly every regular forward is above a 57% expected-goal share on his own line. It also matches every season in the history block, so it is not an early-season mirage.

strengths.title: A record earned by margin
strengths.body: The +33 differential and league-best goal differential per game account for the record. Pts vs Goal Diff is slightly negative, so there is no hidden stash of coin-flip wins waiting to flip back. The longest losing streak is two games. A team that loses this rarely while winning by this much is not living on close games.

strengths.title: Star power plus a deep blueline
strengths.body: Both skater groups grade A+. Andrei Svechnikov is first on the right-wing tab, and Sebastian Aho (26 points) and Logan Stankoven (11 goals) are top-ten centers. On the back end, Shayne Gostisbehere is eighth among defensemen with 14 points. The defense corps holds opposing defensemen well under their own averages, second-best in the league. The talent is spread across lines, so one slump will not sink the offense.

concerns.title: The backup has been a liability
concerns.body: Kochetkov's .920 and +8.7 GSAx carry the team's goaltending. Bussi has given back a big chunk of that in seven starts, at .869 and -4.2 GSAx. Against a team that gives up so few shots, a below-average save percentage is the main way Carolina loses games. Unless Bussi steadies, the crease leans harder on Kochetkov than is ideal over 63 games.

concerns.title: Finishing above its own norm
concerns.body: A 5-on-5 PDO of 102 is well above where this franchise has lived; it sat below 100 in each of the past three seasons. All-situations shooting runs above the league average. Some depth scoring, like Jankowski's goal total on modest shot volume, looks like heat rather than a new level. Expect the goals-per-game figure to drift back toward the low 4s or below even if the chances stay the same.

concerns.title: A merely average power play
concerns.body: For all the five-on-five dominance, the PP sits at 22.2%, 15th in the league and a hair under the league average. History shows this unit swings widely year to year, from 18.7% to 26.9%. This is less a flaw than untapped upside, but it matters in tight playoff games where even-strength edges shrink.

trend.note: Dominant from the start: an 11-3 October, then a 3-1 November with scoring up to 5.5 a game. The last five (4-1-0, +14) only sharpen a level that was already the league's best.

weekAhead.headline: A home-and-home with Seattle, the league's worst possession team
weekAhead.body:
Two games against Seattle, in Seattle on the 12th and back in Raleigh on the 14th. The Kraken's 9-6-1 record flatters them. They are last in the league in shot-attempt share (43%), 27th in expected-goal share and 29th in shots allowed per game. They have stayed afloat on a 103.2 PDO and a positive Pts vs Goal Diff, which is the profile of a team riding its luck. The site has them 26th.

This is close to the ideal matchup for Carolina's style. The Hurricanes should have the puck for long stretches against a defense that already bleeds shots, and Seattle's C- goaltending is not built to survive that. The main ways Carolina drops one are a hot Kraken finishing night or a poor game from whoever is in net. Seattle's shooting has been sharp, sixth in the league.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume against a leaky defense
keyMatchups.body: Carolina leads the league in shots on goal a game, and Seattle allows the fourth-most. The Kraken's goaltending grades C- with a below-average save percentage. Expect Carolina's shot counts to run high in both games.

keyMatchups.title: Carolina's centers against Seattle's middle
keyMatchups.body: Seattle allows centers more points against their averages than any team in the league, and its defense against forwards overall ranks 30th. That sets up Aho and Stankoven, who already lead the club in points and goals, for productive nights.

keyMatchups.title: A chance for the power play
keyMatchups.body: Seattle's penalty kill is 30th at 65.1%. Carolina's league-average power play has a soft target in front of it. A couple of power-play goals in this series would be a useful sign for the one part of the game that has been ordinary.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal. If Bussi gets one of the two, it is a low-risk chance for him to rebuild his numbers against a team that rarely tests its opponent's goalie.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is as solid as foundations get: the best shot share and expected-goal share in the league, consistent with five straight seasons of the same profile. That part does not regress. What does is the finishing. A 102 PDO from a team that has lived below 100 suggests the scoring rate eases and the goal differential narrows toward the levels of recent seasons, still elite but not at the current pace. The 129-point pace becomes something in the 112-122 range, likely a Metropolitan title and a top conference seed.

The real variable is goaltending. With Kochetkov at this level, Carolina can outscore regression on its own. If the starts keep splitting and the backup keeps leaking, the floor drops toward the lower end of the range. The power play is the upside lever; a return toward its better seasons would offset cooling at even strength.
swingFactors: Whether the power play climbs above league average

confidence.note: Only 19 games, but the possession profile matches years of history.
